To address this issue, we developed a novel evaluation metric called Factuality-Preserving Summarization (FPS) that not only identifies existing facts but also detects fabrications made by summarization models. By utilizing FPS, we identified the key limitation of existing summarization models, which is their tendency to distort the original meaning even when factually accurate. To resolve this issue, we introduced a new model called LoyalSum, which combines a factuality-enhancing decoder with a model that preserves the original meaning of the source document. Experimental results demonstrate that LoyalSum significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art model in terms of factuality and summary quality. Notably, LoyalSum's generated summaries are factually accurate 9.2% and 3.4% of the time, surpassing the previous best model by 4.3% and 1.1% respectively. Experimental evaluations utilizing both synthetic and real-world image datasets confirm the superiority of our proposed metric. In recent years, researchers have developed numerous image dehazing techniques, but most rely on complex neural networks that require vast computational resources. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach called Individual Picture Deep Dehazing (IPDDH) has been proposed, which leverages a predictive model to streamline image dehazing. IPDDH empowers users to create personalized haze removal models tailored to specific dehazed images, thus minimizing post-processing efforts. The method involves two key steps: first, a fast image-based haze model is employed to estimate the transmission map, and second, a deep neural network is trained on this map to produce high-quality dehazed images. IPDDH's predictive model enables users to achieve superior results with a mere 0.2% processing time compared to traditional methods, while its effectiveness is comparable to that of leading techniques. The MAJORANA Demonstrator, a highly sensitive experiment designed to detect neutrinoless double-beta decay in germanium, requires precise electron detection and minimal electronic noise. To achieve this, the experiment employs p-type point contacts that convert charge signals into current pulses. A simulation of the pulse shape and noise associated with these contacts in the context of the MAJORARA Demonstrator is presented, revealing that thermal noise in the contact's resistance dominates the overall noise. Utilizing a waveform restoration algorithm, it's possible to recover the original charge signal, enabling the elimination of readout electronics noise and resistance fluctuations. This process effectively removes readout noise by a factor of 10 to 100. Furthermore, the simulation demonstrates the effectiveness of this method in correcting for fluctuations in the contact's resistance. This research highlights the potential of waveform restoration algorithms in minimizing noise for future semiconductor-based experiments. This package enables users to generate simulated pulse shapes, reconstruct charge signals, and visualize noise levels, enabling the optimization of p-type contacts for future experiments. We demonstrate that, for regions whose boundaries comprise simple curves, the 'Connect' problem is, in fact, equivalent to the 'Hamiltonian cycle' problem on a graph derived from the regions' boundary intersections. Consequently, if there are $n$ regions, we can solve 'Connect' in $O(n^2)$ time for simple paths and in $O(n^3)$ time for general region boundaries within polynomial factors of $n$. The concept of learnability barrier refers to the phenomenon where a model trained on a particular dataset fails to perform optimally on another dataset, often due to significant differences in distribution. This issue has been addressed by various research efforts, yet existing solutions are often limited to specific problems and lack a comprehensive framework. Our work introduces a generalized approach to identifying and mitigating learnability barriers in any given dataset, which we call sanctioned learnability barrier. By utilizing the invertible and adversarial alterations of the ImageNet dataset, we can simulate and introduce learnability barriers into existing datasets, effectively creating a new dataset that is both similar and yet distinct. This enables us to develop a comprehensive framework for measuring the impact of learnability barriers on model performance, which can be used to identify and alleviate this issue. Furthermore, we propose a novel method that leverages the invertible and adversarial alterations to train models that are robust against learnability barriers, achieving state-of-the-art results on various datasets. Our approach has the potential to significantly impact the field of computer vision, enabling the development of more robust and adaptable models that can generalize better across different datasets. By doing so, AttDLNet enhances the representation of critical features within the scene, leading to improved localization accuracy. In our AttDLNet, we employ a novel attention module to selectively focus on the most representative points within the scene, and then use a set of feature extraction layers to process the resulting information. To further refine the vehicle's location, we incorporate a novel module that fuses the 3D LiDAR point cloud with a bird's-eye view map. Experimental results demonstrate that AttDLNet significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 6.5% and 7.5% reduction in localization error on KITTI and NOLARDS datasets, respectively. Finally, we examine the algorithm's performance in relation to different subset parameter values and maximum degree limits, discovering that the results are consistent with theoretical expectations. Overall, our findings suggest that the algorithm is a reliable and efficient tool for finding vertex covers in various types of graphs. By leveraging a unique combination of two distinct learning objectives, GClsCR effectively captures both local and global network patterns. The first objective, GClsCR-Local, focuses on identifying local connections by analyzing the similarity between entities, while the second, GClsCR-Global, identifies global structures within the network. To further enhance the accuracy of these predictions, we introduce a new method, called Semantic Correlation Recognition (SCR), which can be applied to any GClsCR variant. Through a combination of this approach, GClsCR-GS+SCR, we can generate multiple predictions for each entity, and then select the most accurate one. Comprehensive experiments conducted on a range of real-world networks demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed method, GClsCR, in comparison to existing state-of-the-art link prediction techniques. Current methods often rely on token similarity, but this approach falls short when dealing with diverse and noisy query keywords. Furthermore, our keyword extraction method can be easily integrated into existing retrieval systems without adding significant computational overhead, making it a practical solution. Additionally, we provide code and data for replication purposes. Our work has the potential to enhance various information retrieval applications, including dialogual search, content recommendation, and related tasks. that has been incorrectly labeled by a system.  Unlike conventional techniques

incorrect inputs itself to generate the corresponding boolean expressions.

equivalent to those created by traditional methods.  Furthermore, experiments
showing the effectiveness of LFM on specific problems reveal that it can
efficiently identify patterns of behavior in scenarios where conventional
approaches are either impractical or produce overly complex expressions.

involves dynamically adjusting the number of incorrect inputs used to generate the
boolean expressions.  This strategy is shown to significantly enhance the
efficiency of LFM.  The research's findings are further validated through the
application of LFM to a real-world problem involving the analysis of a
microcontroller.  The results of this analysis reveal that LFM produces boolean
expressions that are more accurate and efficient than those created by
traditional methods.  Additionally, the experiments show that LFM is capable of
identifying complex system behavior that would be difficult for conventional
methods to detect.  The research's findings are made available as an open-source

behaviors.  The research also presents a new approach to combining LFM with other
abstraction techniques, such as predicate creation, to improve the overall
effectiveness of the abstraction process.  The research's contributions are

findings are expected to have a significant impact on the field of automated

Federated Edge Computing (FEDC) is a promising solution for edge-based machine learning in resource-constrained mobile edge devices. It leverages the interconnected vehicles' computing resources to train a shared model, with each vehicle contributing its local data and computing power. However, the high mobility of vehicles creates a challenge in maintaining effective communication and successful model training. Moreover, the proposed two-stage optimization outperforms a single-stage approach by 1.4 times in terms of model accuracy. This highlights the importance of carefully selecting vehicles and their computations in a highly mobile and densely connected network. This study examines the challenges encountered by agricultural experts in Senegal when assessing crop yields through a method known as the "stripped plot technique". This technique involves measuring the spacing between plants to determine the potential yield of a field. By acknowledging the inherent uncertainty in yield predictions, we have developed a novel approach that incorporates expert feedback to produce more accurate forecasts. Our analysis reveals that agricultural specialists' initial estimates of crop yields are often inaccurate, with estimates falling outside a 20% margin of error approximately 50% of the time. Notably, their predictions are frequently overestimates, resulting in incorrect assessments in nearly 60% of cases. Furthermore, we have found that, in the majority of instances, experts are unable to pinpoint the underlying reasons for their initial mistakes. To address this, we have devised a new statistical method that can provide more accurate yield forecasts with reduced uncertainty. This method has been integrated into a mobile app, allowing users to apply the stripped plot technique with greater precision. Our findings also highlight the need for further research in developing more accurate crop yield forecasting methods that can be adapted to diverse agricultural settings. This study demonstrates the potential for data-driven approaches to enhance decision-making in agricultural practices, particularly in the context of precision agriculture. Speedrunning involves manipulating games to achieve exceptionally high scores within an optimal time. This study presents an innovative framework for reinforcement learning, grounded in the active inference principle. Active inference is a widely accepted theory in neuroscience that views agents as rational agents seeking to minimize uncertainty in their environment. By adopting this approach, agents can be seen as pursuing a fundamental goal: maximising the likelihood of future experiences. Building on this concept, our research demonstrates that by leveraging information gain as a reward function, agents can be trained to achieve optimal outcomes in complex tasks, effectively transforming the active inference framework into a powerful reinforcement learning technique. This novel application of active inference is showcased through its successful use in solving challenging tasks, including balancing an acrobatic drone and navigating a robot in a challenging environment. Our findings indicate that the active inference framework can be successfully adapted for reinforcement learning by integrating it with established methods, resulting in improved task performance. This work has significant implications for the development of more advanced reinforcement learning techniques, potentially leading to the creation of more efficient and robust agents. The proposed framework is made available as an open-source library, designed to facilitate further research in this area. In today's digital age, social media significantly influences how we perceive the world. This issue arises from the fact that rasterization treats each point as an isolated entity, failing to account for the interconnectivity of the 3D mesh. This has led to the development of a novel hypergraph-based method that effectively captures the interconnectivity of the 3D mesh. By leveraging hypergraph learning, the proposed method can effectively reconstruct the 3D mesh, achieving superior results in terms of accuracy, memory usage, and processing efficiency. This is demonstrated through a series of experiments conducted on both artificial and real-world datasets, showcasing the proposed method's exceptional performance. simplified scenarios, which often lack the complexity and variability of real-world

reconstruction methods. The dataset also includes detailed annotations for each image,

reconstruction methods capable of handling real-world complexities. The dataset is
publicly available for research purposes. The accompanying video can be accessed at

A common issue in camera sensors, such as dead pixels, can have a significant impact on image quality. In order to address this problem, we developed a novel method that leverages the efficiency of convolutional neural networks to efficiently identify the location of dead pixels in images. Our approach involves creating a reconfigurable receptive field that allows for targeted pixel analysis without the need for exhaustive image processing. By implementing this technique, we were able to achieve a significant reduction in computational requirements, making it possible to efficiently detect dead pixels in real-time. Our method was thoroughly evaluated through a series of experiments, which demonstrated its ability to accurately identify dead pixel locations while operating at a remarkable 1.2 milliseconds per image. The resulting model, known as DPE, boasts an impressive inference speed of 83 frames per second, making it an ideal solution for a wide range of applications, from real-time dead pixel detection to advanced image processing tasks. Deep neural networks have become essential for mobile edge computing, where they are used for tasks such as object detection and classification. However, the high computational demands of these neural networks lead to significant energy consumption and heat generation, which can cause performance degradation and hardware malfunctions. To mitigate this issue, edge-based devices often employ techniques such as model compression and decomposition to reduce computational demands. However, the resulting models may not be suitable for cloud-based inference platforms. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework, AppealNet, which enables efficient and accurate inference on mobile edge devices by leveraging both edge and cloud resources. AppealNet consists of two models: a compressed edge model and a decompressed cloud model, which are designed to work in tandem to achieve optimal results. The edge model is optimized for real-time inference, while the cloud model is used to provide high-accuracy results when needed. The key innovation of AppealNet is the introduction of an appeal mechanism that allows the edge device to request high-accuracy results from the cloud, which are then combined with the results from the edge device to produce the final output. The appeal mechanism is designed to operate within strict latency constraints, which is achieved through a novel approach that involves dividing the edge device's output into fixed-size patches and sending only the relevant patches to the cloud. The cloud then reassembles the results from the patches to produce the final output. The appeal mechanism is evaluated using a range of experiments, which demonstrate its ability to produce highly accurate results while meeting stringent latency constraints. The results show that AppealNet outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy, while also reducing energy consumption and latency. The AppealNet framework offers a highly efficient and accurate approach to inference, which can be used in a wide range of applications, including object detection, classification, and segmentation. Our analysis of online discussions between supporters of two opposing U.S. Presidential candidates in 2012 reveals how voters engage with one another and how these interactions shape their political beliefs. Through examining more than 180,000 user interactions within a large online forum, we found that the majority of conversations between supporters of different candidates are hostile and infrequent. Our findings indicate that the dynamics between competing candidates closely resemble those of isolated social clusters, with minimal exchange between groups. Our research also suggests that the nature of in-person social connections influences online dialogue patterns, with shared social connections facilitating more frequent and positive interactions between supporters of opposing candidates. Our results have important implications for the potential of constructive dialogue and mutual understanding between supporters of rival candidates and existing models of online conversation. Ultimately, our findings highlight the significance of considering the complexities of face-to-face social connections in online settings. In semi-supervised learning, particularly in computer vision, a significant challenge arises when the quality of pseudo labels generated by a pre-trained model is subpar, significantly hindering the training process. To address this issue, a novel approach called FlexMatch is proposed, leveraging a curriculum learning framework to enhance the quality of pseudo labels. FlexMatch employs a two-stage training strategy, commencing with a stage that optimizes the model's performance on low-to-medium quality data, followed by a stage that refines the model's performance on higher-quality data. The key innovation lies in the use of a curriculum pseudo tagging (CPT) loss function, which dynamically adjusts the difficulty of pseudo labels by comparing the model's predictions against a set of progressively challenging class prototypes. This loss function enables the selection of suitable data for each stage of training, thereby mitigating the negative impact of incorrect pseudo labels. FlexMatch is demonstrated to outperform existing methods in image classification tasks, with a notable improvement of 1.2% on the ImageNet-1K dataset. BERT, a cutting-edge language model, has been adapted for multiple languages. However, the extent to which its cross-lingual capabilities are transferable remains unclear. In this study, we delve into how a pre-trained multilingual BERT model shares knowledge between languages through its shared vocabulary and language-specific embedding spaces. We propose a straightforward method to achieve this alignment through a shared vocabulary and demonstrate its effectiveness in a translation-based data augmentation technique. Furthermore, we show that language-specific embedding spaces can be leveraged for document forecasting in low-resource languages, leading to improved results. Regular physical exercise is a crucial aspect of maintaining physical well-being.  The World Health Organization recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week for adults.  To track this activity, monitoring heart rate is a key indicator.  While specialized equipment is typically used for this purpose, social media platforms often feature videos of users exercising, which can be analyzed using computer vision.  This research aims to develop a method for accurately assessing pulse rate in workout videos by first identifying the user's face and then tracking it.  The face is then segmented into specific areas to estimate pulse rate.  The proposed approach is tested on workout videos from YouTube, which includes 1,000 videos from 75 unique users.  The results show that the method can accurately estimate pulse rate with an average error of 5.1 beats per minute.  The project's code is publicly available on GitHub.

This paper presents a sequence forecasting model designed to predict multiple types of Arabizi output, including transcripts, word segments, and phrases, which are commonly annotated in Tunisian Arabizi data. To achieve this goal, we developed a multi-task sequence forecasting model that leverages the relationships between these different annotations. Our model utilizes a BERT-based encoder to generate sequence representations, which are then used to predict the various annotations at each sequence position. We demonstrate that our model can effectively predict multiple annotations simultaneously, leading to improved results compared to single-task models. Our model was evaluated on a Tunisian Arabizi dataset and achieved state-of-the-art accuracy in predicting transcripts, word segments, and phrases. We also found that our model can generate word segments and phrases that are more coherent and syntactically correct than those produced by single-task models. Our work contributes to the development of sequence forecasting models for Arabizi data and may have broader applications in other sequence forecasting tasks. We release our dataset and code to facilitate further research in this area. We also discuss the limitations of our model and potential directions for future work. We focus on low-rank optimal transport, a generalization of optimal transport theory to high-dimensional data. We develop a comprehensive framework for estimating low-rank optimal transfer matrices, including a novel estimator with a strong empirical error bound. We also investigate the asymptotic properties of low-rank optimal transfer, derive methods for computing and debiasing low-rank optimal transport maps, and provide corresponding empirical results. Notably, our work is the first to establish a strong empirical error rate for low-rank optimal transport, and our estimation and computation algorithms are highly efficient. Moreover, our theoretical and computational analysis of low-rank optimal transport is unprecedented and provides new insights into the field. The stock market's inherent uncertainty is a defining characteristic, resulting in significant price fluctuations on a daily basis.  Predicting volatility has been a long-standing challenge in the finance community, with numerous approaches proposed in recent years.  In this research, we utilize natural language processing techniques to forecast volatility by analyzing news headlines.  Our method involves training and employing a machine learning model that can accurately predict volatility based on financial data, with the model trained on a substantial dataset of 12 years of daily closing prices and corresponding S&P 500 news headlines.  Furthermore, we utilize a unique financial word embedding that can identify meaningful connections between words within the S&P 500 news domain, allowing us to develop a more effective model for volatility prediction.  Our results demonstrate that incorporating this financial word embedding into our model yields a notable improvement in accuracy, with an average relative absolute error reduction of 8.9% and a maximum reduction of 12.2%.  Our findings indicate that leveraging natural language processing techniques can provide valuable insights into stock market dynamics and enhance volatility prediction capabilities. This paper examines a scenario where multiple agents, influenced by nonlinear dynamics and varied perspectives, operate within a network that restricts data transfer between agents, necessitating agreement on a single outcome. We establish a concept of pragmatic agreement in this context, tracking not only the physical state of the network, but also the level of agreement among agents. We then develop a distributed control scheme for agent dynamics that incorporates a control parameter to balance agreement with physical state tracking. The scheme's effectiveness is evaluated through an analysis of its convergence rate, influenced by factors such as communication delays and data transfer limitations. The developed framework is further illustrated through a practical example. The associated code is publicly available.

This paper examines the packing density of disk arrangements within the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, focusing on maximizing the number of disks within a fixed area while maintaining non-overlapping conditions. The upper bound is achieved by placing disks in a grid-like pattern, whereas the lower bound is achieved through a more complex method involving the arrangement of internal points of regular triangles in higher-dimensional spaces. Furthermore, we discuss the potential application of our findings to the field of computer-aided design (CAD) for layered manufacturing processes. Hyperspectral images are highly valued for their rich spectral data, yet their applications are hindered by noise levels stemming from sensor limitations and environmental factors.  To mitigate this issue, various noise reduction techniques have been developed, yet they often neglect the inherent relationships between neighboring pixels in both spatial and spectral dimensions.  To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach called SSCAN, comprising two key components: a spatial-spectral attention module and a spectral-spectral attention module.  The spatial-spectral attention module identifies and amplifies the most informative spatial-spectral relationships among adjacent pixels, while the spectral-spectral attention module amplifies the most relevant spectral-spectral relationships within each spectral slice.  By integrating these modules, SSCAN effectively captures and amplifies the spatial-spectral relationships within hyperspectral images.  Experimental results on three benchmark datasets demonstrate SSCAN's superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods.  The code for SSCAN is available at https://github.com/Chenyu-93/SSCAN. A comprehensive, manually annotated English mixed documents dataset is presented, consisting of 1,000 samples across 46 categories. These categories encompass 14 document types and 32 topic categories, totaling 1,000,000 words. This dataset was created to address the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality datasets for mixed document classification and to provide a more contemporary alternative to existing datasets. These existing datasets, such as the 1998-2002 Govdocs1, are outdated and lack a manual classification system. In contrast, our dataset features a more contemporary and manually curated system, ensuring the accuracy and reliability of its labels. Additionally, its size and scope provide a more comprehensive representation of the challenges associated with mixed document classification. This dataset, Govdocs1K, was used to train and test a range of machine learning models, including a custom model, to evaluate its effectiveness in classifying documents. Our results show that the dataset presents significant challenges for classification, with the best-performing model achieving an F1 score of 0.65. This dataset, along with its code, is available for public use. This research aims to provide a more contemporary and reliable substitute for existing datasets and to facilitate further research in mixed document classification. A key challenge arises from the fact that MARSS models often exhibit non-standard distributional properties, rendering traditional inference methods ineffective. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive framework for calculating standardized residuals within MARSS models. A primary distinction between this work and existing literature lies in the derivation of residuals for models with time-varying parameters, which is a critical consideration in MARSS models. The validity of the proposed approach is demonstrated through a simulation-based evaluation, which reveals that the proposed method yields accurate results in terms of mean and variance. Open information extraction systems have been gaining attention in natural language processing for over a decade, with recent advancements focused on refining their accuracy and expanding their scope. Nevertheless, open data extractors still face a significant challenge in accurately representing the complex meaning of the input text. This limitation stems from the lack of a mechanism to connect extracted concepts to the surrounding context, making it difficult for these systems to scale up to real-world applications. This paper introduces Graphene, a novel open data extraction system designed to address this issue by incorporating a context-sustaining approach. Graphene leverages a graph-based representation of the input text to establish connections between entities, actions, and objects, providing a more coherent understanding of the underlying facts. Our system is evaluated on a range of public datasets, showcasing its ability to generate facts that are both accurate and comprehensive. A detailed analysis of the results highlights the system's capacity for scalability, as demonstrated by its performance on a large-scale dataset of 1.5 million sentences. In the field of neuromorphic photonic integrated circuits, optical matrix multiplication plays a crucial role. A common component in these systems is the 2D photonic integrated circuit, capable of performing matrix multiplication on a large scale. Training neural networks with large numbers of parameters requires optical matrix multiplication, driving the need for efficient frameworks that can be easily optimized. This paper compares the performance of three frameworks, MatPyTorch, PyTorch-PI, and OptML, to train optical matrix multiplication in neuromorphic photonic integrated circuits. The frameworks were tested on a 1024x1024 optical matrix multiplier and found to have varying levels of difficulty in achieving convergence. MatPyTorch and OptML were able to converge, but OptML was more efficient due to its ability to leverage the same photonic circuit. In contrast, PyTorch-PI struggled to converge, but its ability to handle complex systems was still beneficial. Ultimately, the choice of framework will depend on the specific requirements of the system, with MatPyTorch and OptML being more suitable for large-scale training, and PyTorch-PI being better suited for complex systems. This paper provides valuable insights for researchers working on neuromorphic photonic integrated circuits. The concept of pathway smoothing, where the trajectory of a control system is smoothed, has been explored in the context of nonlinear control systems. This smoothing process involves modifying the system dynamics to make it more stable. In this research, we examine the effect of pathway smoothing on the behavior of neural networks. We demonstrate that pathway smoothing converts a neural network's output layer into a quadratic programming problem, and we establish conditions for when a neural network solution exists. This solution existence depends on the network's hidden dynamics and output function. We also establish a connection between pathway smoothing and quadratic programming, and we show that pathway smoothing converts a control system into a more stable system. This stability is measured using the quadratic Lyapunov function. To illustrate the effectiveness of pathway smoothing, we apply it to a neural network controller for a double pendulum and a quadrotor, and we show that it leads to improved performance. This improved performance is achieved through reduced oscillations and better tracking capabilities. Additionally, we apply pathway smoothing to a neural network for a cartpole system, and we show that it leads to improved robustness against disturbances. This robustness is achieved through the reduction of the effect of disturbances on the system. To facilitate further research, we provide MATLAB code for implementing pathway smoothing on a neural network. This code is available on the repository https://github.com/ozanaytac/pathway_smoothing. We also provide an open-source implementation of the pathway smoothing algorithm in the Python package https://github.com/ozanaytac/pathway_smoothing. This package includes a Python implementation of the pathway smoothing algorithm and a Python implementation of the pathway smoothing algorithm for a double pendulum and a quadrotor. The package also includes a Python implementation of the pathway smoothing algorithm for a cartpole system. The objective of open-set identification is to determine when a sample does not belong to a known class. This task is crucial for ensuring safety in real-world applications, where misclassifying an unknown sample could have severe consequences. Current methods for open-set identification are often based on the mean and variance of feature representations, but these approaches lack the ability to adapt to new, unseen classes. In this research, we propose a novel open-set identification framework that leverages self-supervised learning to generate synthetic data from known samples and then uses a classifier to predict whether an input is from an unknown class. This approach is based on the assumption that a well-trained model should be able to recognize known samples among the synthetic data. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, outperforming existing methods across different settings. Additionally, our framework provides a new perspective on the open-set identification task and enables the development of more sophisticated and accurate approaches for this problem. We introduce a novel approach for creating synthetic light field images that capture accurate depth information, utilizing a cost-effective design. Our method leverages the capabilities of a standard camera array to produce high-quality depth maps, and we demonstrate its potential through the creation of a low-cost, occlusion-aware expense generator. Furthermore, we present a method for estimating the cost of producing synthetic images based on real-world data captured by a standard camera array. Our solution is validated through experiments conducted using various camera array configurations, and the results show that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of depth accuracy and cost-effectiveness.
